A 50-year-old man is diagnosed with a gastrinoma in his pancreas.
There is no evidence of metastases.
Which of the following is the ﬁrst treatment of choice?
explanation:
Surgical resection is the treatment of choice for localised disease and offers the possibility of cure in up to 25% of patients.
A Whipple's procedure offers the best chance of effecting cure but excellent long term survival in those with less extensiveprocedures means that these may be considered for less advanced, smaller tumours.
Chemotherapy is useful in those patients with metastatic disease not suitable for surgery.
Treatment with PPIs is useful in controlling features of the disease resulting from excess acid production (ulceration, diarrhoea).

A patient is diagnosed with cholangiocarcinoma. They have a staging CT which states that the tumour involves both the conﬂuence of theright and left hepatic ducts with tumour involvement in both ducts.
Which type of cholangiocarcinoma is this according to the Bismuth-Corlette classiﬁcation?
explanation:
The Bismuth-Corlette classiﬁcation is as follows:Type I - below conﬂuence of left and right hepatic ductsType II - reaching conﬂuence but not involving left or right hepatic ductsType III - occluding common hepatic duct and either right (IIIa) or left (IIIb) hepatic ductType IV - multicentric or bilateral intrahepatic segmental involvement; or involving conﬂuence and both right and left hepaticducts.
It is commonly used but does not take into account factors such as distant metastases or vessel involvement.

You review a 26-year-old woman in the gastroenterology clinic. She was previously treated with omeprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycinfor Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori).
She remains on PPI therapy but continues to have epigastric discomfort. You suspect she has ongoing H. pylori infection and request a ureabreath test to investigate this.
How long would the patient need to stop her PPI therapy before the urea breath test?
explanation:
Urea breath testing is a non-invasive test for H. pylori.
It uses C or C labelled urea. C labelled urea is the more commonly used method and requires the patient to be off PPI therapy
for 14 days.
Urea breath testing has 90% sensitivity and 96% speciﬁcity in the diagnosis of H. pylori.
Reference:
Bloom S, Webster G. Oxford Handbook of Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2nd ed. Oxford: Oxford University Press; 2006.

A 35-year-old woman who was diagnosed with hepatitis C six months ago has attended follow up in the gastroenterology clinic.
She reports dry eyes and asks if this could be related to her hepatitis C.
Which of the following is an extrahepatic association of hepatitis C?
explanation:
This woman is likely to have Sjögren's syndrome, which is an extrahepatic association of hepatitis C.
Porphyria cutanea tarda, rather than acute intermittent porphyria, is associated with hepatitis C. Lichen planus, rather than lichensclerosis, is another known cutaneous association with hepatitis C.
Hepatitis C is associated with haemotological disease and malignancy. Cryoglobulinaemia (mixed essential type) is the most well-recognised of these with its attendant cutaneous, neurological and renal complications.
Hepatitis C is also associated with myeloma and monoclonal gammopathies rather than Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia.
Lymphoma, rather than leukaemia, is another extrahepatic association of hepatitis C.
Reference:
Bloom S, Webster G. Oxford Handbook of Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2nd ed. Oxford: Oxford University Press; 2006.

A 63-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive airways disease is reviewed in clinic. He has been complaining of longstandingdyspepsia which has been worsening.
He is on long term low dose prednisolone, aminophylline and Seretide for his airways disease. Alendronate has been started for boneprotection. He also takes nifedipine for hypertension and allopurinol as prophylaxis against gout.
According to NICE guidelines on the management of dyspepsia which of his oral medications is least likely to be contributing to hissymptoms?
explanation:
Drugs are a common cause for dyspeptic symptoms. Dyspepsia may be the result of the action of drugs on gastric mucosa (forexample, steroids, NSAIDs) or as a result of smooth muscle relaxation causing incompetence of the lower oesophageal sphincter (forexample, calcium channel blockers, nitrates).
The following drugs are recognised as causing dyspepsia:SteroidsCalcium channel blockersTheophyllinesNitratesBisphosphonates, andNon-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs.
This is either due to irritation of the mucosa (for example, bisphosphonates, steroids) or relaxation of the lower oesophagealsphincter increasing reﬂux (for example,  calcium channel blockers, nitrates).

A patient presents with perianal itch, tenesmus, and bloody discharge. Examination in clinic reveals ﬁrm bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy.
Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lesions below the dentate line that are malignant will drain via the skin lymphatics to the inguinal nodes. Therefore, cancers such asanal squamous cancer or anal malignant melanoma will result in lymphatic spread to the inguinal nodes.
Anal intraepithelial neoplasia is a pre-malignant condition and as it has not penetrated the basement membrane is localised bydeﬁnition and will not cause lymphadenopathy.
Low rectal cancer will spread via the mesorectum to the internal and para-aortic nodes.
Benign conditions will not usually present with lymphadenopathy.

A 44-year-old man is noted to have abnormal liver function tests. He denies regular alcohol intake.
On examination he is confused, there is no asterixis. Abdominal examination reveals 3 cm hepatomegaly.
Which of the following blood results is characteristic of alcoholic liver disease?
options: AST more than twice the level of ALT
explanation:
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) more than twice the level of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) is characteristic of alcoholic liverdisease.
Often the ALT is normal or only very mildly elevated, an ALT >1000 should raise the possibility of an alternative diagnosis such asischaemia or drug toxicity.
An isolated raised alkaline phosphatase should raised the possibility of biliary disease ﬁrst and foremost. Though it may be elevatedin alcoholic liver disease it is not characterisitic of the condition.  A low albumin may be found in liver disease, malnutrition or chronicillness of any cause and ALT > AST is not a speciﬁc feature of alcoholic liver disease.
Reference:
Bloom S, Webster G. Oxford Handbook of Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2nd ed. Oxford: Oxford University Press; 2006.

A 75-year-old retired farmer from mid-Wales was found to have very mildly deranged liver function tests during a routine health check up.
He had an ultrasound scan which demonstrated multiple cystic lesions in the right lobe of the liver ranging in size from 1-8 cm in diameter.The larger cysts have a calciﬁed appearance.
He had a melanoma removed from his back 20 years ago and has had multiple basal cell carcinomas removed from his head, face, and armsin recent years.
Which investigation should be carried out next?
explanation:
Asymptomatic, calciﬁed cystic lesions in the liver are typical of hydatid cysts.
Hydatid infection was endemic in sheep farming regions (such as Wales or New Zealand) in the past and sheep dogs were infected byeating infected offal. Humans contract hydatids via faecal/oral spread from dogs.
The liver cysts are usually asymptomatic and calciﬁcation usually denotes a non-viable cyst.
Ultrasonography is probably the most helpful initial test since it can usually differentiate a simple cyst from other cystic lesions. Itshould also be used for follow up studies.
Hydatid serology has a sensitivity of 80-90%. If hydatid serology is negative then further imaging (CT/MRI) +/- aspiration may berequired to make a diagnosis.
Melanoma metastases are not typically cystic and calciﬁed.

According to the British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines on the management of ascites what is the most appropriate way to managethis gentleman's hyponatraemia?
options: Stop diuretics and give normal saline
explanation:
Patients with chronic liver disease and ascites often develop hyponatraemia, the management of which can be diﬃcult. Diuretictherapy for the management of ascites often contributes to the hyponatraemia.
The British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines suggest that where the serum sodium is ≤ 120 mmol/L diuretic therapy should bestopped and patients should receive volume expansion with colloid or normal saline.
These guidelines also advise that ﬂuid restriction should only be used in patients who are clinically euvolaemic, not on diuretics andhave severe hyponatraemia with a normal serum creatinine.

options: Incubation of infection with hepatitis B
Recovery from infection with hepatitis B
Acute liver failure caused by hepatitis B
explanation:
This pattern of serology suggests vaccination against hepatitis B.HBsAg is detected in high levels in serum during acute of chronicHBV infection. The presence of HBsAg indicates that the person is infectious. The presence of anti-HBs is generally interpreted asindicating recovery and immunity from HBV infection. Anti-HBs also develops in a person who has been successfully vaccinatedagainst hepatitis B. 
The presence of anti-HBc indicates previous or ongoing infection with HBV in an undeﬁned time frame.
Anti-HBe's presence indicates that the virus is replicating and the infected person has high levels of HBV. It is produced by theimmune system temporarily during acute HBV infection or consistently during or after a burst in viral replication. Spontaneousconversion from e antigen to e antibody (a change known as seroconversion) is a predictor of long-term clearance of HBV in patientsundergoing antiviral therapy and indicates lower levels of HBV.

She wants to discuss interferon and ribavirin therapy and whether or not it is likely to be effective.
Which one of the following is a predictor of a favourable long term response to interferon?
explanation:
The most important predictor of response to interferon therapy is the genotype of the hepatitis C virus being treated. Genotypes 2and 3 have a far better response to treatment than genotype 1.
Beyond this female patients are more likely to show a long term response to interferon treatment.
The following also predict a good long term response to interferon:Non-black racial originLow hepatic ironAbsence of cirrhosis on biopsy, andYounger age.

A 52-year-old patient with ulcerative colitis comes to clinic to discuss the results of a screening colonoscopy. Mild disease activity was notedto the splenic ﬂexure with a mild sigmoid stricture.
Which follow-up regime should be offered?
options: Encouraged to present symptomatically and participate in bowel cancer screening at the appropriate age
explanation:
Due to the presence of a stricture, this patient falls into a high risk category and should receive a colonoscopy in one year.
Current British Society of Gastroenterology (BSG) guidance suggests that colonoscopic screening of all colitics should commence10 years after diagnosis. Screening colonoscopies should be undertaken during a period of disease quiescence and ideally with pan-colonic dye-spray.
High risk features are:moderate or severe active inﬂammationstricture in the past 5 yearsdysplasia detected in the last ﬁve yearsPSC, orsigniﬁcant family history.
Reference:
Cairns SR, Scholeﬁeld JH, Steele RJ, et al. Guidelines for colorectal cancer screening and surveillance in moderate and high riskgroups (update from 2002). Gut. 2010;59:666-689.

A 78-year-old male is admitted with lower abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and elevated serum lactate. An abdominal CT scan shows left-sidedcolitis from the distal transverse colon with sparing of the lower half of the rectum.
Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The distribution of the colitis described is the same as the distribution of blood supply to the colon via the inferior mesenteric artery,making ischaemic colitis the most likely cause. Elevated serum lactate also suggests ischaemic aetiology.
Crohn's colitis could present in such a way although an index presentation with left-sided colonic disease only in a patient of this ageis unlikely. Infective colitis is also possible although this would normally be pancolonic.
Radiation colitis commonly occurs as a side effect of treatment of pelvic cancers (male - prostate, female - gynaecological) andusually affects the rectum. Ulcerative colitis would not be expected to spare the distal rectum.
The initial treatment would be resuscitation and referral to surgery for consideration of colectomy if the situation does not improve.

Abdominal examination, including a rectal examination, is unremarkable. He did not take any regular medication and had not been usingnon-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory agents.
On the advice of his GP he had stopped smoking and improved his diet.

options: Omeprazole 20 mg once daily for one month
Omeprazole 20 mg b.d., clarithromycin 500 mg b.d. and amoxicillin 1 g b.d. for one week
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and rapid urease test
explanation:
In a patient aged below 55 years the symptoms of heartburn which is exacerbated by fatty foods and the recumbent position in theabsence of alarm features such as vomiting, bleeding, anaemia, unexplained weight loss, abdominal mass, or dysphagia makes thediagnosis of gastro-oesophageal reﬂux disease (GORD) the most likely.
In this patient group, NICE guidelines suggest if lifestyle changes are ineffective that a one month course of a proton pump inhibitor(PPI) is given or a test and treat strategy for Helicobacter pylori is employed. If one is ineffective then the other may be tried (with useof prokinietic or H2RA in the case of use of PPI after H. pylori eradication). Urea breath testing rather than glucose breath testing isused to detect the presence of H. pylori.
There is no evidence that either oesophago-gastroduodenoscopy (OGD) or H. pylori testing is indicated in these patients.

NICE. Gastro-oesophageal reﬂux disease and dyspepsia in adults: investigation and management (CG184).

A 17-year-old boy of white Irish parents is admitted with haematemesis.
Gastroscopy demonstrates bleeding oesophageal varices.

Hepatic wedge pressure− 6 mmHg (<7)
Inferior vena cava− 3 mmHg (<5)

explanation:
The normal hepatic venous pressure gradient (normal HVPG = 1-5 mmHg) means that the portal hypertension is not related to post-sinusoidal intrinsic liver disease such as cirrhosis (caused in children by metabolic disorders such as A1ATD) or post-hepatic venousobstruction (HV thrombosis).
The HVPG is calculated by subtracting the free hepatic venous pressure (which reﬂects intra-abdominal pressure) from the wedgedhepatic venous pressure (which reﬂects portal venous pressure). These values are obtained by hepatic venous catheterization. Thehaemodynamic goal of treatment is reduce the HVPG by 20% or to less than 12 mmHg, using a non-selective beta blocker. If this isnot achievable despite titrating the beta blocker dose, then endoscopic variceal ligation must be considered.
The obstruction must be pre-sinusoidal.
Sarcoidosis is a very rare cause of pre-sinusoidal portal hypertension, particularly in white children.
Schistosomiasis is the leading cause of pre-sinusoidal hypertension worldwide but is unlikely in an Irish boy.

A 67-year-old woman presents complaining of worsening bloody diarrhoea and abdominal pain. She describes bloody diarrhoea for the lasttwo weeks and also abdominal discomfort worsened by eating.
She has a past medical history of hypertension and angina. She is currently taking aspirin, simvastatin and bisoprolol. She has recently beentaking ibuprofen for both the abdominal and some joint pain.
On examination she has a pulse of 102 bpm, which is irregular, blood pressure is 112/54 mmHg, temperature 37.6°C and there is some mildtenderness in the left iliac fossa. A ﬂexible sigmoidoscopy shows ulceration of the mucosa involving the descending colon to the splenicﬂexure with rectal sparing and a number of diverticula.
What is the most likely cause for her symptoms?
explanation:
This patient has signiﬁcant risk factors for atherosclerotic disease and there is clinical evidence of atrial ﬁlbrillation (a potentialsource of emboli).
The preceding history of abdominal pain exacerbated by eating is suggestive of mesenteric ischaemia. Pain that isdisproportionately severe compared to the abdominal ﬁndings is characteristic. The ﬁnding of ulceration which spares the rectum istypical and ulceration extending to the splenic ﬂexure corresponds with the arterial supply of the inferior mesenteric artery.
Diverticulitis does not give rise to widespread mucosal ulceration.
The lack of risk factors and clear demarcation of the areas ulceration count against a diagnosis of infective colitis.
NSAIDs may cause colitis or exacerbate a pre-existing colonic disease but the mechanism is unclear. Patients experience bloodydiarrhoea, weight loss, fatigue, and chronic iron deﬁciency anaemia. When the drug is discontinued, the colitis improves.

You review a 45-year-old man in the gastroenterology clinic who has been referred by his GP with abnormal liver function tests. The only pastmedical history is a recent diagnosis of diabetes mellitus.
On direct questioning he denies alcohol intake or intravenous drug use. There is no travel history.
On examination he is tanned, there is evidence of clubbing and he has spider naevi over the anterior chest wall. Abdominal examinationreveals tender hepatomegaly 4 cm below the costal margin.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Clinical signs of haemochromatosis include hepatomegaly, cirrhosis and splenomegaly. Patients may have cardiomyopathy andendocrine complications including diabetes mellitus, hypogonadism, panhypopituitarism and testicular atrophy. The term 'bronzediabetes' comes from the skin pigmentation which is seen in these patients. Chondrocalcinosis and arthritis may also develop.Hepatocellular carcinoma should be excluded especially in those with cirrhosis with three to six monthly alpha fetoprotein andultrasound.
Many patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease are asymptomatic. The diagnosis is usually made by incidentally raisedaminotransferases or ultrasound scan demonstrating a fatty liver. Right upper quadrant pain may be reported and patients oftenhave hepatomegaly.
Primary biliary cirrhosis is a cholestatic disorder which affects middle-aged women in 90% of cases. There is an association withautoimmune diseases. Patients have stigmata of chronic liver disease; other clinical signs include xanthelasma and excoriations as aresult of pruritus.
Primary sclerosing cholangitis is associated with inﬂammatory bowel disease. Patients often present with pruritus, intermittentjaundice and right upper quadrant pain. Features of cholangitis (fever, pain and jaundice) usually occur subsequent toinstrumentation such as endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). Examination reveals signs of chronic liverdisease and signs of portal hypertension may be present.

She reports noticing some blood mixed with stool but mostly in the pan and on the paper. She also describes bloating, alternating diarrhoeaand constipation with some urgency and tenesmus. She has had the problem intermittently for the last ﬁve months, she reports no systemicsymptoms and her weight is steady.
Her medications consist of senna and the oral contraceptive pill.

explanation:
Haemorrhoids are the most likely cause of this lady's symptoms and are by far the most common cause of painless rectal bleeding.The patient is taking senna and there is a history of constipation with which haemorrhoids are associated.
Anal ﬁssures may give rise to fresh rectal bleeding but they are associated with pain upon defecation.
Diverticular disease is a possibility but would be very unusual in a patient of this age, not typically developing until the sixth toseventh decade of life.
The history includes a number of symptoms which are suggestive of a diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome; however rectalbleeding is not a feature of this condition and suggests another concomitant diagnosis.
Ulcerative colitis typically presents with chronic passage of bloody diarrhoea. Where disease is limited to proctitis patients can beconstipated but still lose blood and mucous per rectum.

The pain frequently occurred at night and was associated with an acidic taste in the mouth. He had found some relief by taking over-the-counter antacid tablets and had seen his GP who prescribed a proton pump inhibitor. However, despite a two month course of omeprazolethe patient was still experiencing frequent episodes of chest discomfort. His GP had also sent blood for Helicobacter pylori serology whichwas found to be negative.
He was otherwise well and did not give a history of any weight loss, vomiting or dysphagia. There was no other past medical history of note.
On examination, he looked well. He was not clinically anaemic. His pulse was 80 beats per minute and regular with a blood pressure of135/70 mmHg. His heart sounds were normal and the chest was clear. His abdomen was soft and non-tender with no palpableorganomegaly or masses. A rectal examination was unremarkable and normal stool was noted on the examination glove.
An outpatient upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was arranged. This revealed a 10 cm area at the lower oesophagus that had the appearanceof non-inﬂamed Barrett's epithelium. Multiple biopsies were taken. The histology was reported as columnar lined mucosa with intestinalmetaplasia. No dysplasia was seen.
What advice should be given?
options: Start a proton pump inhibitor and repeat the endoscopy and biopsy in two years
Repeat the endoscopy and biopsy in two months
Start a proton pump inhibitor and repeat the endoscopy in ﬁve years
explanation:
The histology is typical of Barrett's oesophagus.
The risks of adenocarcinma are relatively high (30 × normal) but absolute risk is low 1% per year develop adeno-carcinoma.
This patient has no dysplasia and so at present, we would start a PPI and re-scope in two years. This is appropriate in an otherwisehealthy person, the merits of surveillance need to be assessed on a patient to patient basis. (For example, would the patient tolerateany intervention?)
Evidence for PPI is not great but is recommended by guidelines.

A 65-year-old woman presents with a one month history of progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids. She is not sure whether she has lostany weight.
There is no past medical history. She is a smoker but denies regular alcohol intake. On examination she appears pale and thin, her abdomenis soft and non-tender and there are no palpable masses.
Which of the following is the next best investigation to aid the diagnosis?
explanation:
The likely diagnosis is a malignant oesophageal stricture given the patient's age and rapidly progressive nature of the dysphagicsymptoms.
Endoscopy allows tissue diagnosis from biopsies and brushings and has a 98% detection rate in oesophageal carcinoma. Endoscopyalso allows dilatation and/or stent placement where dysphagia is severe or the stricture is impassable. Endoscopy would also permitdiagnosis of many of the differential causes of dysphagia in this case. It is therefore the the next best investigation here..
Barium swallow is useful but does not have the beneﬁt of allowing a histological diagnosis which is key in this case.
Barium swallow may be the initial investigation where dysphagia is not severe or if the patient has previously been diagnosed with astricture and the site is known. It is also likely to be more helpful where a motility disorder is suspected.
A chest x ray is helpful to identify mediastinal lymphadenopathy or aspiration, but endoscopy is the investigation of choice in makingthe diagnosis.
An air-ﬂuid level may also be seen on chest x ray but its presence indicates obstruction rather than a speciﬁc underlying cause.
A staging CT scan will be required after the diagnosis is made; endoscopy the more important in obtaining histology.
Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is better than CT or MRI for assessing lymphadenopathy, staging mural invasion and assessingsuitability for surgery in patients with oesophageal carcinoma.

explanation:
Current British Society of Gastroenterology (BSG) guidance suggests that acromegalics should undergo colonoscopic screening withthree yearly colonoscopy in the presence of either elevated IGF-1 or adenomas at initial screening. High risk features are detection of adenomas or elevated IGF-1 which should prompt three yearly follow-up, otherwise colonoscopycan be deferred for ﬁve years. Low-risk patients can be offered colonoscopy every 5-10 years.

A 37-year-old woman presents with tiredness and lethargy, she denies any other symptoms.
Her blood tests show that she is anaemic. Her haemoglobin is 103 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 76 fL, ferritin 5 µg/L and anti-tissuetransglutaminase antibodies are negative.
She is concerned as her father was diagnosed with bowel cancer at the age of 72 and her maternal grandfather died of bowel cancer at theage of 80.
According to the British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines on the management of iron deﬁciency anaemia what is the most appropriatecourse of action?
explanation:
This lady is young and very likely to be pre-menopausal. In such patients blood loss through menstruation is by far and away themost common cause of iron deﬁciency anaemia. British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines on the investigation andmanagement of iron deﬁciency anaemia advocate that following a negative coeliac screen, and in the absence of uppergastrointestinal symptoms or a signiﬁcant family history of bowel cancer, no further gastrointestinal investigation is warranted and atrial of iron replacement should be instituted.
Any suggestion of extra-gastrointestinal disease or blood loss should, of course, be investigated as appropriate. Failure to respond toiron replacement should trigger consideration of further investigation.
Colonoscopy (or CT colonoscopy) would be indicated only if there was a signiﬁcant family history of bowel cancer. According to theBSG guidance, a signiﬁcant family history is considered to be "two affected ﬁrst-degree relatives or just one ﬁrst-degree relativeaffected before the age of 50 years".
She is both signiﬁcantly anaemic and iron deﬁcient meaning that adjustments to diet are likely to be inadequate to produce aresponse.

A patient presents with constipation that is thought to be functional.
Which of the following symptom sets fulﬁls Rome III diagnostic criteria?
options: Straining and lumpy stools 10-20% of the time for six months
Alternating periods of hard stools with loose stools in between for several years
Recurrent abdominal pain relieved by defecation
Straining and sensation of obstructive defecation for most bowel motions for six months
A sensation of incomplete emptying all of the time without other symptoms for 6 months
explanation:
Straining and sensation of obstructive defecation for more than 25% of stools without looser stools and features of IBS would fulﬁlRome III criteria as long as symptoms had been present for three months with symptom onset greater than six months.
The Rome III criteria for functional constipation is as follows (it must include two or more of the following):straining during at least 25% of defecationslumpy or hard stools in at least 25% of defecationssensation of incomplete evacuation for at least 25% of defecationssensation of anorectal obstruction/blockage for at least 25% of defecationsmanual manoeuvres to facilitate at least 25% of defecations (e.g., digital evacuation, support of the pelvic ﬂoor)fewer than three defecations per weekloose stools are rarely present without the use of laxatives, andinsuﬃcient criteria for irritable bowel syndrome.
These criteria must be fulﬁlled for the last three months with symptom onset at least six months prior to diagnosis.

The motions are semi-formed with blood mixed within it. He described gripping abdominal pain and felt unwell. He had continued to attendlectures. His father had ankylosing spondylitis and uveitis.

explanation:
A deceptive question - and one that illustrates that care needs to be taken when reading the precise instruction.
There is no doubt that the presentation is highly suggestive of inﬂammatory bowel disease with the family history and probableerythema nodosum.
However, it is unforgivable not to do a stool culture in a case of diarrhoea and that should be the starting point before consideringthe other investigations, particularly as the duration of the history is acutally relatively short making an infective cause more likely.

A 57-year-old man becomes unwell on the ward with visual hallucinations, profuse sweating and tremors. He was admitted three days agowith diarrhoea, which has now resolved.
He has a previous history of alcohol and intravenous drug abuse. His pulse is 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 190/90 mmHg andtemperature 37.8ºC.
On examination he is agitated, sweaty and inattentive with multiple spider naevi on his trunk and jaundiced sclerae. He has mild ascites and anon-tender abdomen and the chest is clear on auscultation. A liver ﬂap cannot be elicited.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Delirium tremens is the most severe form of alcohol withdrawal.
Onset is typically three to seven days after cessation of chronic alcohol ingestion. It is characterised by visual hallucinations,autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension, and pyrexia), obtundation and confusion. Sweating, tremors and agitation are alsofeatures.
Hepatic encephalopathy tends to be characterised more by drowsiness and obtundation. Signiﬁcant hepatic encephalopathy isunlikely to be present if a liver ﬂap (asterixis) cannot be detected.
Opiate withdrawal is characterised by diaphoresis, shaking, cramping, agitation and diarrhoea. Autonomic instability andhallucinations are not features of opiate withdrawal.
Sepsis would need to be excluded in a case such as this however the patient is hypertensive rather than hypotensive and neither thehistory nor examination reveals evidence of a particular source of infection.

Other than depression there is no past medical history. He is vegetarian but reports a full and varied diet. Blood tests performed demonstratethat his haemoglobin is 108 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 81 fL and ferritin 15 µg/L. He is concerned regarding his anaemia and what mustbe done.

explanation:
This gentleman has signiﬁcant anaemia with biochemical evidence of iron deﬁciency (low serum ferritin). Post-menopausal womenand all men with evidence of iron deﬁciency anaemia require further evaluation and consideration of investigation to excludegastrointestinal cancer.
According to the British Society of Gastroenterology guidance patients with marked anaemia (<120 g/L in men and <100 g/L inwomen) should be referred urgently as lower levels of haemoglobin reﬂect more severe disease.
It is unlikely that an iron deﬁcient diet will explain the degree of anaemia and iron deﬁciency in this man. Vegetarian diets need notbe lacking in iron if suﬃciently varied.
Reassurance or watch-and-wait (re-check haemoglobin later) are not appropriate options in this gentleman who has a marked irondeﬁciency anaemia.
Whilst a trial of oral iron may well result in an improvement in haematological and biochemical markers it will not help elucidate theunderlying cause which must be determined.

A 46-year-old woman complains of profuse diarrhoea. She also mentions when questioned ﬂushing, particulary in association with theconsumption of red wine.
On examination a pansystolic murmur is heard over the praecordium, loudest at the lower left sternal edge.
Excess of which compound is the likely cause of her diarrhoea?
explanation:
The case described is classical of carcinoid syndrome. The syndrome is caused by excessive levels of serotonin secreted from aneuroendocrine tumour arising from enterochromaﬃn cells in the gut or less frequently the lung. Carcinoid syndrome occurs inmetastatic disease as the liver metabolises the hormones secreted by gut limited disease. The excessive release of serotonin causessymptoms of diarrhoea and right-sided cardiac valve disease. Tumour production of histamine, tachykinins and/or prostaglandinsmay give rise to ﬂushing and itching. Precipitation of symptoms by alcohol is common.
Vasoactive intestinal polypeptide is over-produced by VIPomas which cause chronic, profound watery diarrhoea.
Gastrin is produced by G cells of the stomach, its over-production leads to excessive acid production and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
Somatostatin producing tumours are extremely rare, the classical pentad of symptoms is diabetes, steatorrhoea, gallstones, weightloss and achlorhydria. Patients may also experience symptoms related to mechanical obstruction - biliary or duodenal.Somatostatinomas are associated with neuroﬁbromatosis.
Cholecystokinin producing tumours are extremely rare.

explanation:
The presentation and histology are consistent with a gut associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) lymphoma or gastric MALToma.
These are almost always associated with and driven by Helicobacter pylori infection - a positive Campylobacter-like organism testindicates this is present. Helicobacter eradication therapy (antibiotics and proton pump inhibition) is effective in producing diseaseregression in around 75% of cases of low-grade disease associated with infection.
Treatment with surgery, chemotherapy or radiotherapy has not been demonstrated to be superior to antibiotic therapy. Where thelatter has failed radiotherapy has been shown to be effective and is used where the tumour can be captured in a single radiotherapyﬁeld.
Surgery has only a limited role in the treatment of gastric MALToma. Chemotherapy is occasionally used in the treatment of GALTlymphoma and the regimes used are similar to those used for low-grade non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.
Fluorouracil-based chemotherapy is typically used in the treatment of gastric adenocarcinoma.

Her full blood count shows her to have a haemoglobin of 103 g/L and her C reactive protein is <5 mg/dL.
According to the British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines on the management of iron deﬁciency anaemia which of the following is themost sensitive marker for iron deﬁciency?
explanation:
The serum ferritin is the most powerful marker of iron deﬁciency in the absence of inﬂammation. Ferritin is an acute phase reactantand may be grossly elevated in the context of acute inﬂammation (when it does not accurately reﬂect iron stores) and to a lesserdegree in chronic inﬂammation.
British Society Guidelines on the diagnosis and management or iron deﬁciency anaemia suggest that a cut-off of 12-15 mg/Lreﬂects iron deﬁciency in the absence of inﬂammation. Where inﬂammation is present a ferritin of 50 mg/L or more may still becompatible with iron deﬁciency.
Hypochromia (reduced mean corpuscular haemoglobin) and microcytosis (reduced mean corpuscular volume) are both red cellchanges which accompany iron deﬁciency. They may be inﬂuenced by concomitant B and folate deﬁciencies however.
Serum and total iron binding capacity are not felt to be as powerful markers of iron deﬁciency as serum ferritin. A mathematicalcombination of serum ferritin and total iron binding capacity has been shown to be more effective in identifying iron deﬁciency thaneither test alone in the setting of chronic disease.
Reference:
British Society of Gastroenterology. Guidelines for the Management of Iron Deﬁciency Anaemia.

explanation:
Dysphagia is an 'alarm' symptom and needs prompt investigation. Rapidly progressive dysphagia suggests a malignant stricture;progressive dysphagia and weight loss are often the presenting features of oesophageal carcinoma. Additionally there is no priorhistory of acid reﬂux symptoms (though this may be absent in up to 25% of peptic strictures). Smoking and alcohol are both riskfactors for squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus.
Achalasia is rare - the incidence is approximately 1 in 100,000 in the west. It typically presents with dysphagia and odynophagia.Patients with achalasia have regurgitation which may cause nocturnal cough.
Peptic ulcer disease is a common cause of chronic abdominal pain.
In duodenal ulceration abdominal pain often improves with food intake whereas in gastric ulcers pain is typically exacerbated byeating.

Atkinson RJ, et al. Medical Masterclass: Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2nd ed. London: Royal College of Physicians; 2008

A 67-year-old woman is admitted with jaundice and right upper quadrant pain.
Abdominal ultrasound scan demonstrates a gallstone in the common bile duct with evidence of intrahepatic bile duct dilatation. She is dueto undergo endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) for biliary sphincterotomy and stone extraction.
According to the British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines on the management of common bile duct stones (2008), what is the most
common procedure-related complication?
explanation:
Pancreatitis is both the most well known and most common complication of ERCP, estimates of incidence range from 1.3% to 6.7%.Different patient populations do have different risks of developing this complication. Female sex, age less than 60 and a lowprobability of structural disease (suggested by a normal bilirubin, non-dilated ducts or suspected sphincter of Oddi dysfunction) allincrease the risk.
Cholangitis is a signiﬁcant risk in those with obstructive jaundice or CBD stone and occurs in around 1% of cases (estimates rangefrom 0.5% to 5%).
Gastrointestinal haemorrhage is reported in 0.7-2% of cases, the need for biliary sphincterotomy will increase the likelihood ofbleeding as a complication (1.5% in recent BSG audit data).
Duodenal perforation is surprisingly common with estimates of incidence ranging from 0.3% to 1%.
Cardiorespiratory complications, predominantly related to sedation, are a mixed group of conditions and are not infrequent (0.5-2.3%).
Reference:1. Williams EJ, et al. Guidelines on the management of common bile duct stones (CBDS). Gut. 2008;57:1004-1021.

A 61-year-old old lady was referred to clinic by her GP with a six month history of fatigue. There was no history of weight loss or change inbowel habit, no cough or sputum production.
She denied having any fevers or sweats. Her only other complaint was of occasional pains in her joints secondary to rheumatoid arthritis,which had been diagnosed three years previously.
She worked as an assistant in a bookshop and lived with her husband. She had three children, all of whom were well. There was no familyhistory of note. She was a lifelong non-smoker and seldom drank alcohol.
On examination she appeared well. She was afebrile. Xanthelasma were noted around both eyes. A few faint scratch marks were visible onthe skin of her arms. She attributed this to an 'allergy' to a new washing powder.
Her pulse was 70/min with blood pressure 110/65 mmHg. Heart sounds were normal with no murmurs or added sounds. Her chest wasclear. The abdomen was soft and non-tender. The spleen was palpable 3 centimetres below the left costal margin. The liver and kidneys werenot palpable. Neurological examination was normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Over 90% of cases of primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC) occur in women aged 35 to 70.
The presentation is usually insidious. Pruritus, non-speciﬁc fatigue, or both are the initial symptoms in more than 50% of patientsand can precede other symptoms by months or years.
About 50% of patients present with an enlarged, ﬁrm, non-tender liver; 25%, with splenomegaly; about 15%, with skin xanthomas;and 10%, with hyperpigmentation.
Jaundice is present in 20% of patients and tends to develop in others with time.
Clubbing, metabolic bone disease (that is, osteoporosis), peripheral neuropathy, renal tubular acidosis, and steatorrhea (from thecholestasis and pancreatic secretory failure) are possible. Later, all the features and complications of cirrhosis can develop.

A 38-year-old man presents with frank haematemesis. He does not speak English therefore you are unable to obtain a history.
On examination he is shocked with a heart rate of 110 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 95/70 mmHg. There is evidence of palmarerythema and spider naevi. Abdominal examination reveals ascites and splenomegaly with epigastric tenderness.
Which of the following is the next best step in the immediate management of this patient?
explanation:
For the initial resuscitation of patients with an upper GI bleed take an ABC, that is, airway, breathing, circulation approach. Establishgood intravenous access ideally two 14-16 G cannulae in the antecubital fossae. If there is haemodynamic compromise, administercolloid or crystalloid and review the response. The haemoglobin may not fall immediately as this occurs only after reactive plasmavolume expansion and haemodilution. If there is signiﬁcant bleeding cross-match 2-8 units.
In cases of massive exsanguinating blood loss and delay in the availability of cross-matched blood, administer uncross-matchedgroup O Rh negative packed red cells.
Do not attempt insertion of a central venous pressure (CVP) line before initial resuscitation as failure and complications are morelikely - use large-bore peripheral cannulae. A CVP line can be considered at a later stage in major haemorrhage especially if there ispoor response to initial resuscitation.
This patient has portal hypertension and he has presented with what is likely to be an acute variceal bleed. Terlipressin is importantin the management of variceal bleeds. Give 2 mg IV stat followed by 1- 2 mg every four to six hours for 72 hours or until the bleedingstops. It is contraindicated in patients with known vascular disease or an ischaemic ECG. Terlipressin helps control haemorrhage andmay reduce mortality but it does not replace the necessity for endoscopy.
In a suspected acute variceal haemorrhage endoscopy should be performed as soon as possible - ideally this should be once thepatient has been resuscitated and is haemodynamically stable but this may not be achievable in someone who continues actively tobleed from their varices.

explanation:
The 2013 British Society of Gastroenterology (BSG) guidance on endoscopic surveillance of Barrett's oesophagus recommends thatendoscopy should be performed every three to ﬁve years for patients with a <3 cm segment of Barrett's without dysplasia. For longersegment Barrett's (>3 cm) without dysplasia the recommended interval between endoscopies is shorter (two to three years).
Patients with low grade dysplasia should have high dose acid suppression and endoscopy six monthly until dysplastic changeresolves (then as per no dysplasia) or high grade dysplasia is noted.

A 59-year-old woman presents with ongoing dyspeptic symptoms despite taking 40 mg of omeprazole for eight weeks.
Four weeks previously she underwent gastroscopy which revealed widespread inﬂammation of the lower third of the oesophagus with twoerosions. Helicobacter pylori testing was negative.
What is the next most appropriate course of action?
options: Double dose of proton pump inhibitor for one month
Add an H2 receptor antagonist to treatment
Refer for acid reﬂux reduction surgery
Continue on current dose of proton pump inhibitor for a further month
explanation:
In endoscopically determined gastro-oesophageal reﬂux disease or oesophagitis full-dose proton pump inhibition for one month willtypically result in healing in 76%, continuation for a further month increases this by a further 14%. In those failing to respond to twomonths of full dose therapy doubling the dose of proton pump inhibitor increases response rate.
In those failing to respond to a double dose of proton pump inhibition an H2 receptor antagonist may be added or substituted intreatment or a prokinetic agent added to treatment. Simply extending the duration of proton pump inhibitor therapy beyond twomonths without any additional change is not recommended.
Repeat gastroscopy is not recommended in the absence of new or emergent symptoms or where there is severe resistance totherapy.
It is also the latter group in whom referral for consideration of acid reﬂux reduction surgery might be considered.
Reference:
NICE. Gastro-oesophageal reﬂux disease and dyspepsia in adults (CG184).

On examination she looked thin but well. Apyrexial no lymphadenopathy the chest was clear, heart sounds normal and abdominalexamination including per rectal examination was unremarkable
What would be the most appropriate investigation to perform next?
explanation:
The history is pointing towards malabsorption with fat stools that ﬂoat, generalised small bowel disease and pancreatic disease areboth in the differential.
Giardia is seen in child care setting and also abroad. It is faeco-orally transmitted and can be carried without symptoms. In general itis a short (ﬁve to seven days), chronic infection occurs but this lady is generally well and a 7 day course of metronidazole would becurative in at least 90% of cases.
There may be underlying small bowel pathology, for example, coeliac, so a small bowel biopsy would give a deﬁnitive answer. Aserological screening test for coeliac would be the most appropriate next test, as per guidance on the evaluation and diagnosis ofCoeliac disease prior to arranging upper GI endoscopy and small bowel biopsy.
Her mother has scleroderma, but she herself does not, so bacterial overgrowth is unlikely.

A 37-year-old homeless gentleman with a history of alcohol excess presents to hospital with painless and progressive abdominal distension.Examination reveals shifting dullness. An ascitic tap is performed and the ﬂuid sent for analysis.
According to the British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines on the management of ascites what is the best measurement to use in orderto classify the nature of the ascitic ﬂuid and understand the possible cause?
explanation:
The serum ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) is considered the most sensitive and speciﬁc method of categorising ascites. Tocalculate the ascitic ﬂuid albumin should be subtracted from the serum albumin.  A value that is ≥ 11 g/L (high SAAG) indicates atransudate (e.g. cirrhosis, cardiac failure), <11 g/L (low SAAG) indicates an exudate (e.g. malignancy, pancreatitis).
A ﬂuid total protein cut-off level of 25 g/L has been used to categorise ascitic ﬂuid as transudative or exudative.
However, using this to categorise ascites means that in different patients ascites due to the same cause may be variously deemed tobe either an exudate or a transudate.
Measurement of ﬂuid lactate dehydrogenase may be used as part of the application of Light's criteria to determine whether pleuralﬂuid is an exudate or transudate.
Measurement of the ﬂuid amylase is advised where pancreatic disease is thought to be the cause of ascites.
Application of the ﬂuid albumin in isolation is not useful in categorising ascites.

He attended for endoscopy due to a history of six weeks of dyspeptic symptoms and associated weight loss. He has a previous history ofosteoarthritis for which he takes regular ibuprofen.
His gastroscopy report describes a 3 cm, clean-based ulcer with ﬂat edges in the gastric antrum. The rapid urease (Campylobacter-likeorganism) test was positive. He wants to know what effect Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy, in addition to acid suppression, will haveon his peptic ulcer disease.
Which of the statements below most accurately describes the advice he should be given?
options: Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy increases ulcer healing but does not affect the chances of recurrence
Helicobacter pylori eradication will not affect the chances of ulcer healing but will decrease ulcer recurrence
Helicobacter pylori eradication will have no effect on either ulcer healing or recurrence
Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy is not indicated for this gentleman
Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy will increase ulcer healing and will signiﬁcantly decrease ulcer recurrence
explanation:
In patients taking non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy does not increase the chances ofulcer healing when compared to acid suppression alone but does reduce the chances of recurrent peptic ulceration.
This gentleman has a peptic ulcer with benign appearances (ﬂat as opposed to rolled edges).
A positive CLO (Campylobacter-like organism) test indicates the presence of Helicobacter pylori.
Eradication therapy is indicated in the context of peptic ulcer disease as it increases healing rates and reduces recurrence and isrecommended by the NICE guidelines on Dyspepsia (CG184).
The size of the respective effects is dependent upon whether ulceration is gastric or duodenal and whether the patient is takingnon-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs or not.
For duodenal ulcers eradication slightly increases healing (additional 5.4% over acid suppression alone) but dramatically decreasesrecurrence (increases the number of patients ulcer free at 12 months by 52%).
For gastric ulcers eradication therapy has no effect on healing but does decrease recurrence (an additional 32% of patients are ulcerfree at 12 months compared to acid suppression alone).

explanation:
Patients who are positive for HBsAg for more than six months but are HBeAg negative, HBV DNA negative and have normal ALT donot require liver biopsy nor do they require antiviral therapy, but hepatitis B serology and ALT should be monitored annually.
A liver biopsy would be undertaken where the liver function tests are persistently abnormal; there are imaging (US or ﬁbroscan),clinical or biochemical features to suggest signiﬁcant ﬁbrosis with elevated HBV DNA levels (typically <2000 IU/ml).
Abnormal LFTs with undetectable or very low HBV DNA levels would merit consideration of biopsy, however one would need to thinkabout alternative reasons for abnormalities in the liver enzymes and this may be the main reason for biopsy.
Antiviral would not be indicated unless biopsy suggested signiﬁcant disease due to HBV.

explanation:
Haemorrhoid grading guides treatment. It is based on prolapse and whether or not this returns spontaneously, requires manualreduction, or is permanent.

Second degree haemorrhoids prolapse on defecation and return spontaneously while third degree require manual reduction.
Fourth degree haemorrhoids are permanently prolapsed.
Full thickness rectal prolapse would not be described as occurring at a particular point as it would be circumferential and typicallyoccurs in older female patients.

You review a 34-year-old woman in the gastroenterology clinic.
She is known to have Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and has been undergoing regular colonoscopy surveillance.
How often should colonoscopy screening be carried out?
explanation:
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder with an incidence of 1:50,000 live births.
Patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome require colonoscopy every two years after the age of 25 for evaluation of the presence ofpolyps and polypectomy.
The disorder which predisposes to the carcinoma is caused by mutations in the LKB1 gene. Patients characteristically havemucocutaneous pigmentation with hamartomatous polyps predominantly affecting the small bowel and also the stomach andcolon.
There is an association with non-gastrointestinal malignancies such as endometrial, ovarian and lung.

explanation:
The problem with drugs in pregnancy, like drugs in children, is that few have been formally assessed and are not licensed. Howeverin the clinical setting treatment is often given.
Clearly this lady does not need an endoscopy, in fact it is doubtful she ever needed an endoscopy.
Reassurance is reasonable however unlikely to be effective.
Antacids and alginates are widely used and as far as is possible to tell are safe.
The next step is H2 blockers; again they have been used and have not been found to be harmful however no direct trials exist.
With PPI there are conﬂicting reports, with some case series of accidental exposure showing no harm, with other case reports raisingsuspicion. This will need to be discussed with the patient.

A 47-year-old man is admitted for a colonoscopy and polypectomy.
He is currently taking warfarin following diagnosis of a pulmonary embolism four months ago. He also has chronic renal impairment with aneGFR of 25 mls/min. His most recent INR was taken one week ago and the result was 2.7
According to the 2008 BSG guidelines on the management of anticoagulants at endoscopy what is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Stop warfarin and admit for UFH infusion when when INR <
Stop warfarin and bridge with LMWH when INR <2
Continue warfarin but at a lower dose aiming for INR 1.5-2
Stop warfarin ﬁve days prior to endoscopy and ensure INR <1.5
explanation:
Colonoscopy with polypectomy is an endoscopic procedure which carries a high risk of haemorrhage.
Venous thromboembolism more than three months ago is considered a low risk clinical scenario for temporary discontinuation ofanticoagulation.
Where the endoscopic procedure carries a high risk of bleeding and the indication for anticoagulation is low risk for discontinuationthen anticoagulation should be discontinued until the INR is <1.5 and restarted post-procedure. Bridging with heparin is notrequired.
Bridging is only recommended if the indication for anticoagulation is high risk - for example, mechanical mitral valve, atrial ﬁbrillation(AF) and prosthetic valve, recent venous thromboembolism (VTE) (less than three months), thrombophilia.
Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) is relatively contraindicated in patients with an estimated glomerular ﬁltration rate (eGFR) lessthan 30 mls/min, these patients may require admission for unfractioned heparin (UFH) infusion depending upon local policy andpractice.
Where an endoscopic procedure is associated with a low risk of haemorrhage then the BSG recommends continuation ofanticoagulation at the current dosage providing an INR within the last seven days is within the therapeutic range.
Aiming for a raised but sub-therapeutic INR is not recommended in any situation.

explanation:
Patients with gastric ulceration tend to suffer from anorexia and weight loss while those with a duodenal ulcer maintain or gainweight.
Although weight gain may be suggestive of duodenal ulceration the characteristic clinical feature which aids the diagnosis isabdominal pain which is relieved by eating. Endoscopy should be performed to conﬁrm ulceration.
Risk factors for peptic ulceration include Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection, non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drug (NSAID) use,cigarette smoking and genetic factors - Lewis blood group antigens facilitate H. pylori attachment to the mucosa.

A 50-year-old man with known alcoholic liver disease is noted by the nursing staff to be confused on the ward. On examination he istachycardic with a heart rate of 100 beats per minute, his blood pressure is stable at 122/85 mmHg.
He is alert, there is no asterixis but his family who are also present report some change in his mood and behaviour.
Abdominal examination reveals ascites with generalised abdominal tenderness.
What is the severity of this patient's hepatic encephalopathy?
explanation:
There are ﬁve grades of hepatic encephalopathy:Features of grade 0 encephalopathy include minimal alterations and impairment of executive function.If patients are drowsy they have at least grade 1 encephalopathy. Grade 1 encephalopathy is associated with sleepabnormalities (typically sleep inversion) and changes to behaviour and personality (irritability, poor concentration).Lethargy, apathy and drowsiness are features of grade 2.Depressed conscious levels (but rousable) are a feature of grade 3 encephalopathy.In grade 4 patients are comatose with no response to painful stimuli.
Confusion covers a huge range of clinical features and is a fairly poor descriptive term. Note in the criteria listed that grade 1 and 2disease includes inappropriate behaviour and some disorientation to time and place - many people would refer to this as confusion.The key feature of increasing encephalopathy is depression of the conscious level.
Reference:
Travis SPL, et al. Pocket Consultant Gastroenterology. Oxford: Blackwell Publishing; 2005.

A patient who is new to the area attends your clinic for the ﬁrst time.
You read his medical notes. He has had gastric hamartomas, which is the reason he is attending a gastroenterology clinic. He has a history ofbasal cell carcinomas, mandibular bone cysts, and intracranial calciﬁcation as well as pits on the palms of his hands.
Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Gorlin syndrome causes gastric hamartomas, basal cell carcinomas, mandibular bone cysts, and intracranial calciﬁcation, as well aspits on the palms and soles.
Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is caused by a mutation in the APC gene and is associated with the formation of multipleadenomatous polyps in the colon. By the age of 35, around 95% of patients with FAP have polyps and, without colectomy, coloncancer is effectively inevitable. Extra-colonic manifestations are variable and include polyps of the gastric fundus and duodenum,osteomas, dental anomalies, and congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE).
Juvenile polyposis syndrome is characterised by a tendency to form hamartomatous polyps throughout the GI tract. Juvenile refersto a particular type of polyp rather than the age of the patients at the onset of polyp formation (though most have polyps by the ageof 20). Inheritance is autosomal dominant. There is an increased risk of GI cancer mostly attributable to an excess of colon cancer.Estimates of lifetime risk of GI cancer are variable and range from 9-50%.
Peutz-Jehgers syndrome is characterised by the association of hamartomatous GI polyps and mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation.PJS-type hamartomas are most frequently found in the small bowel but also occur in the stomach, colon, and nasal passages.Patients with PJS are increased risk of both stomach and colon cancers arising from adenomas in addition to other cancers such aspancreatic, breast, and ovarian malignancy.

A 28-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department, jaundiced and unwell with a distended abdomen.
He is awaiting a liver transplant secondary to alcoholic liver disease and has been abstinent from alcohol for the past 18 months. Syntheticfunctions of the liver reveal decompensation with INR 1.8, albumin 16 g/L, and bilirubin 109 μ mol/L.
He is pyrexial and you suspect spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
What is the single best treatment for his albumin in the ﬁrst instance?
explanation:
Cirrhotic ascites has signiﬁcantly lower protein and complement levels than non-cirrhotic ascites. This can result in less opsonicactivity of the peritoneal ﬂuid predisposing to spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
Albumin replacement treatment is warranted in this diagnosis and can also decrease the development of the hepatorenalsyndrome.
The salt-poor preparation of albumin is particularly important in this scenario as high salt load will encourage ﬂuid to shift into theextravascular compartment resulting in ﬂuid overload.

A 53-year-old woman becomes unwell on the ward with visual hallucinations, sweating and tremors. She was admitted four days ago withdiarrhoea which has now resolved.
She has a previous history of alcohol and heroin abuse. Her pulse is 130 beats per minute, blood pressure 190/80 mmHg and temperature37.9ºC.
On examination she is agitated, sweaty and inattentive with jaundiced sclerae. She has mild ascites and a non-tender abdomen and the chestis clear on auscultation. A liver ﬂap cannot be elicited.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Delirium tremens is the most severe form of alcohol withdrawal. Onset is typically three to seven days after cessation of chronicalcohol ingestion.
It is characterised by visual hallucinations, autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension, pyrexia), obtundation and confusion.Sweating, tremors and agitation are also features. This is the likely diagnosis in this case and treatment is with benzodiazepines.
Antibiotics would be appropriate if there were signs of infection however there is no evidence in the history or examination tosuggest a particular source.
Methadone would be an appropriate treatment for opiate withdrawal.
High dose vitamin B replacement would be an appropriate treatment for Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.
Haloperidol may be used in the sedation of patients who are distressed and anxious and present a danger to themselves or othershowever in delirium tremens it may lower the seizure threshold and has no effect on the underlying pathophysiology.

On examination he is tachycardic with a heart rate of 100 beats per minute; his blood pressure is stable at 122/85 mmHg. He is drowsy andconfused. Abdominal examination reveals ascites with generalised abdominal tenderness. He has asterixis.
You diagnose hepatic encephalopathy secondary to spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
Which of the following is the least appropriate management step in the management of hepatic encephalopathy?
explanation: There is little evidence for the role of protein restriction in hepatic encephalopathy. This may exacerbate the condition as thesepatients are often malnourished.

A 56-year-old male with metastatic oesophageal cancer on palliative chemo presents with nausea and vomiting which has been gettingworse for two months despite antiemetic treatment. He describes episodes of vomiting which are worse after eating and occasionally hasvomited up formed parts of meals he has ingested recently. A diagnosis of oesophageal obstruction secondary to local tumour invasion ismade and the patient is stented successfully before being discharged home later that week with a nasogastric feeding regime.
One week after being discharged he presents to the accident and emergency department with dysphagia and worse vomiting from his initialpresentation with regurgitation of whole food. He states to have stuck to the diet plan almost entirely apart from a small piece of chickenwhich he insists he chewed thoroughly.
Bloods are unremarkable.
Chest X-Ray is unremarkable.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Worsening local invasion should not be occurring this soon after stent insertion and would be accompanied with other symptoms ofgeneral deterioration and weight loss. 
Achalasia presents with dysphagia to solids and liquids and on barium swallow produced a classical bird beak appearance. It is due tothe inability of the lower oesophageal sphincter to relax; this is not mentioned here.
Paraneoplastic phenomena are a diagnosis to consider but dysphagia from oesophageal cancer is not widely recognised. Stentmigration is a possibility but given the hint towards the patient taking on solid food earlier than ﬁrst though it is more likely that foodimpaction is the cause of this patients acute dysphagia and vomiting.
